title: Buttons, suppliers and method references
summary: Runnable and BooleanSupplier bind buttons to actions; method references name a method to run later.

say.never: You don't have to write a new interface for every lambda. Java comes with ready-made ones in `java.util.function`. The name tells you the shape. A `Runnable` takes nothing and hands back nothing: it just *does* something (`run()`). A `BooleanSupplier` takes nothing and hands back true or false (`getAsBoolean()`). A `DoubleSupplier` hands back a number (`getAsDouble()`). A `Consumer` takes a value and keeps nothing. A `Function` takes a value and hands one back.

A robot checks its buttons about 50 times a second. If the action ran every time the button *is* down, one press would run it dozens of times. So you remember what the button was last time, and act only when it's down now but wasn't before. That moment is called a **rising edge**. A doorbell works the same way: one ring per push, however long you hold it.
say.bit: Act on the **rising edge**: true now, false last time. Then remember the value.

steps.title: In your lesson: Only on the way down

say.never: `onTrue` only *remembers* the pair: add a `new Binding(condition, action)` to `bindings_`. `poll()` loops over every binding. Ask its `condition_` for `getAsBoolean()`. If that's true and `was_true_` is false, call `action_.run()`. Then save the value in `was_true_`, pressed or not.
say.bit: `onTrue`: `bindings_.add(new Binding(...))`. `poll`: per binding, run `action_` on a rising edge, then update `was_true_`.

say.never: Your turn! Write `onTrue` and `poll()`. Remember: `onTrue` never runs the action itself.

Lots of lambdas just call one method that already exists, like `() -> speaker.beep()`. Java has a shorter way to say that: `speaker::beep`. Read `::` as "the method called". There are no parentheses after `beep`, because you're not calling it now. You're naming it so it can be called later. `Math::abs` works the same way for a method that takes a number.
say.bit: `object::method` is short for a lambda that just calls that method. No `()`: it's named, not called.

board.code:
Runnable beep = speaker::beep;       // () -> speaker.beep()
BooleanSupplier late = clock::isLate; // () -> clock.isLate()
DoubleUnaryOperator size = Math::abs; // x -> Math.abs(x)

say.never: A `DoubleSupplier` doesn't hold a number. It holds *how to get* one. Each `getAsDouble()` runs the lambda again, so you get today's temperature, not the one from when the program started. If a lambda needs to pass a value to the method, like `setVolume(3)`, write a normal lambda instead of a method reference.
say.bit: A supplier reads a fresh value on every call. Need to pass a number? Use a lambda, not `::`.

marks.label: needs a value, so a lambda

say.never: `controller_.a()` hands back true or false and takes nothing, so `controller_::a` is a `BooleanSupplier`. `intake_.run()` takes nothing and hands back nothing, so `intake_::run` is a `Runnable`. Bind B to `intake_::stop` the same way. X needs `setPower(EJECT_POWER)`, which takes a number, so it gets a lambda. Then make `driveSpeed()` return a lambda that reads the stick, flips its sign and passes it through `stick_filter_`.
say.bit: `buttons_.onTrue(controller_::a, intake_::run);`, the same for B, a lambda for X, and a stick-reading lambda in `driveSpeed()`.
